title: Level Design Workflow 🎨
description: Go from concept to greybox and assemble your first beautiful scene.

slides.title: The Level Designer’s Mindset 🧠
slides.content:
# Think Before You Build

Great levels don’t happen by accident. They follow a process:

1. **Concept** – reference images, rough layout on paper
2. **Blockout (Greybox)** – build the shape with simple cubes
3. **Asset Replacement** – swap grey shapes for final art
4. **Lighting & Atmosphere** – set mood
5. **Polish** – details, sound, optimisation

Today we’ll focus on steps 1‑3.

slides.title: Greyboxing – Your Secret Weapon 🧱
slides.content:
## Build Ugly, Then Build Beautiful

Greyboxing means blocking out your level using only basic shapes (cubes, cylinders) from the **Place Actors → Shapes** menu.

Why?
* **Fast** – no waiting for art
* **Playtest early** – check scale, flow, gameplay
* **Flexible** – easy to move walls before details are final

*Analogy:* An architect builds a foam‑core model before constructing a real building.

Use **M** to open the Material Browser and apply a grey grid material to your blockout shapes for uniformity.

quizData.question: Why is greyboxing recommended before placing final assets?

options.text: It lets you test scale and flow quickly
It is required by the engine

quizData.explanation: Greyboxing enables rapid iteration on layout without waiting for art assets.

slides.title: Composition & Scale 📐
slides.content:
## Guiding the Player’s Eye

Use composition techniques:
* **Leading Lines** – roads, rivers, railings draw the eye
* **Framing** – arches, windows, or trees highlight a focal point
* **Rule of Thirds** – place key objects at intersections of an imaginary 3×3 grid

**Scale is critical.** In Unreal, 1 unit = 1 cm. A typical character is ~180 units tall. A door should be ~210 units high, ~100 wide. Build a reference cube (200×200×200) as a scale ruler.

Common scale mistakes: rooms too small, doors too short. Measure everything against your reference character.

slides.title: Modular Asset Thinking 🧩
slides.content:
## Build Like LEGO

In professional game art, environments are made from **modular pieces**: wall sections, floor tiles, pillars, doorways – all designed to snap together.

When building, think: “Can I reuse this piece?” A single wall mesh can be duplicated to make a whole room. This is efficient and keeps visual consistency.

In Unreal, use **grid snapping** (10 or 100 units) so modular pieces align perfectly.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Use the BSP Brushes

For quick greyboxing, Unreal includes **BSP Brushes** (Place Actors → Geometry → Box). These are not final geometry but great for prototyping. You can carve holes, add/subtract space, and later convert to Static Meshes.
